endorsements.quote: In practical terms, this may involve the establishment of dedicated Clinical AI Oversight Committees with multidisciplinary representation, including clinicians, data scientists, ethicists, legal scholars, and patient advocates [ 50 ].
Academic institutions can generate independent evidence, characterize model limitations, and inform federal standards.

Evaluation pipelines should include (1) external validation across settings and populations, (2) stress-testing for dataset shift and performance drift, and (3) explicit reporting of failure modes and subgroup performance because model behavior frequently changes across time, sites, and workflows [ 48 ].

To improve transparency and comparability across studies, AMC-led evaluations should follow reporting guidelines appropriate to the study type: TRIPOD+AI (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis—AI) for prediction-model studies [ 45 ], CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials–AI) for clinical trial reports [ 46 ] or SPIRIT-AI (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials–AI) for clinical trial protocols [ 47 ].

Many industry actors have also strengthened internal validation and compliance infrastructures; however, independent academic evaluation remains essential to mitigate structural conflicts of interest and to preserve public credibility [ 24 , 25 ].

Operationalizing this stewardship will require transparent governance frameworks, clearer conflict-of-interest policies, and institutional mechanisms that prioritize patient welfare over commercial incentives.

At a minimum, every deployed clinical AI tool should have a short “AI label” or model card adapted to clinical practice, stating intended use, population, training and validation cohorts, known failure modes, and required clinician oversight.
That label should be paired with a local implementation dossier that specifies workflow integration points, override expectations, and a monitoring plan with explicit triggers for reassessment.
Importantly, prespecified triggers linked to accountable action convert postdeployment monitoring from passive observation into an active safety process.
Importantly, governance should extend beyond initial approval to continuous monitoring, recognizing that model performance may drift as data distributions evolve [ 48 ].

They can set a standard that procurement is conditional, not final: clinical AI tools are adopted provisionally, audited as they are used, and can be restricted or removed when monitoring reveals unacceptable performance.

At the undergraduate level, AI literacy should emphasize 3 competencies: understanding model architecture at a conceptual level, recognizing common failure modes (including hallucination and bias amplification), and developing structured verification habits [ 53 ].
Faculty development programs should establish baseline AI governance competencies for attending physicians responsible for supervision and evaluation.

Integrate AI literacy and adversarial model evaluation throughout undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, and continuing medical education, emphasizing clinical reasoning alongside AI outputs

Consequently, each educational stage is tied to a proposed assessment approach: case-based critiques of AI-generated clinical reasoning, structured “human-in-the-loop” exercises in UME, supervised use with documented override decisions during GME, and formal audit-style or portfolio assessment in CME.
publish institutional AI governance charters defining decision-making authority and accountability
AMCs should evaluate whether clinical AI performs equitably across the populations they serve [ 19 , 20 ].

Shared benchmark datasets, shared evaluation protocols, and pooled approaches to postdeployment monitoring reduce duplication and improve external validity without requiring each institution to build an assurance laboratory from scratch.

AMCs can start with a narrow portfolio of high-stakes systems, treat oversight as part of the patient safety infrastructure, and adopt a governance charter that defines procurement conditions, audit intervals, and escalation pathways.

This includes establishing standards for AI procurement, protecting patient privacy, ensuring human oversight in clinical decision-making, and addressing the algorithmic biases that can perpetuate health disparities.
Targeted microcredentials maintain workforce competencies as models and testing pipelines evolve.

unlisted_practices: Protect independence of academic AI evaluations through institutional firewalls, transparent funding, and the right to publish null or unfavorable findings without sponsor interference.
Embed AI literacy and competency-based assessment across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education.
Develop precompetitive joint labs and shared benchmark datasets with industry and across institutions.
Track institutional progress metrics such as proportion of faculty with AI safety training and share of deployed models passing institutional evaluation.
Provide oversight groups with authority to condition procurement and require revalidation, rather than only recommend.
Integrate AI oversight into existing quality and safety infrastructure and M&M conferences.
